headline: Walmart’s third quarter: profit grew three times faster than sales, and the full-year outlook went up again
takeaway: Revenue rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion and adjusted EPS of $0.65 edged past the $0.64 analysts expected. The more important line is further down: operating income grew 16%, advertising 25% and membership fees 17%, and Walmart raised its full-year sales, profit and EPS guidance for the second time this year.
results: Walmart reported revenue of $188.8 billion for the quarter ended October, up 5.2%, or 4.5% at constant currency. Adjusted earnings per share were $0.65 against a consensus of about $0.64 and $0.62 a year earlier; on a reported basis EPS was $0.62, the difference being a loss on equity investments that Walmart excludes.

Operating income rose 16.0%, or 5.5% on the adjusted constant-currency basis the company guides to, and the gross profit rate widened by 28 basis points. Global e-commerce sales grew 17% and the US business grew 23% online. Walmart US comparable sales rose 2.9% excluding fuel, with transactions up 1.5% and average ticket up 1.4%; Sam’s Club comparable sales rose 4.9%.

Cash flow was the soft spot. Operating cash flow for the year to date was $29.4 billion, up $2.0 billion, but free cash flow fell $2.0 billion to $6.8 billion as capital spending rose, and inventory was up 8.1% — which Walmart attributes to strategic initiatives, the timing of seasonal events and cost inflation.
mgmt: John Furner, in his first full quarter as chief executive, described the results as the core business growing and gaining market share, and pointed to membership, ‘agentic shopping’ and new uses of the store and delivery network as the next sources of growth. Walmart launched a bundle combining Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus for $120 a year during the quarter.

The company raised its fiscal 2027 guidance: net sales growth of 4.9% to 5.2% at constant currency (previously 4.0% to 5.0%), adjusted operating income growth of 8.0% to 8.6% (previously 7.0% to 8.5%) and adjusted EPS of $2.84 to $2.89 (previously $2.80 to $2.87). That is the second increase since the original outlook in February.

Two items distort the comparisons and management flagged both. The timing of Flipkart’s Big Billion Days sale moved out of the quarter, which cut International sales growth by about five percentage points with the benefit expected in the fourth quarter. And in the US, price deflation in health and wellness tied to the maximum fair price drug regulation took roughly 70 basis points off comparable sales.
view: The number that explains Walmart’s valuation is not the 5% sales growth, it is the gap between sales and profit growth. Operating income grew three times faster than revenue, and the reason is mix: advertising grew 25% globally and 37% in the US, membership fee revenue grew 17%, and the marketplace keeps scaling. Those lines carry margins many times higher than selling groceries, and each point of mix shift toward them lifts the profit of a business with $700 billion of sales. This quarter is the clearest evidence yet that the shift is continuing rather than maturing.

The underlying retail engine is healthy but slowing from an exceptional base. US comparable sales of 2.9% compare with 4.5% a year ago, and the health and wellness deflation explains only part of the difference. Transactions rising 1.5% matter more than the headline: customers are visiting more often, which is what share gain looks like in grocery. E-commerce adding roughly 530 basis points to the comp says store-fulfilled delivery is now the growth engine, and improved e-commerce economics were named as a reason US operating income grew 9%.

What deserves scrutiny is cash and inventory. Free cash flow down $2.0 billion while inventory rises 8.1% — faster than sales — is the combination that precedes markdowns when demand softens. Management’s explanation is credible, and excluding Flipkart inventory is growing slower than sales, but a retailer heading into the holiday quarter with inventory growing ahead of revenue has less room for a demand surprise. Capital spending at about 4% of sales, raised earlier in the year, is the other reason cash conversion is lower.

On valuation the debate does not change. Walmart trades on a multiple that assumes the advertising and membership businesses keep compounding, and this quarter supports that assumption. The risk is not the retail business; it is paying a technology-style multiple for a company whose core still earns a low-single-digit margin. A raised guide for the second time in a year is what the bulls needed. The Sam’s Club operating income decline of 16%, partly from the new bundle’s accounting, is a reminder that buying membership growth has a cost that will run through results until it is lapped next year.
watch: Fourth-quarter inventory and the holiday comp. If inventory growth drops back below sales growth and the Flipkart timing benefit arrives as promised, the quarter’s one weak spot disappears; if not, margin gets tested in the quarter that matters most.
